'''Bernard Flood Burke''' (June 7, 1928&nbsp;– August 5, 2018) was an American astronomer. He co-discovered [[radio emission]] from [[Jupiter]], and was part of the team that discovered the first [[Einstein ring]] in 1988.

== Early life ==
Burke was born on June 7, 1928<ref name="nrao_papers">{{Cite web|url=https://www.nrao.edu/archives/Burke/burke.shtml#Biography|title=Finding Aid to the Papers of Bernard F. Burke, 1959–2004: Biography|last=Bouton|first=Ellen N.|website=National Radio Astronomy Observatory|publisher=Associated Universities, Inc. National Science Foundation|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180810042207/https://www.nrao.edu/archives/Burke/burke.shtml#Biography|archive-date=August 10, 2018|url-status=live|access-date=August 11, 2018}}</ref> in [[Brighton, Boston]].<ref name="obituary2">{{Cite web|url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/bostonglobe/obituary.aspx?n=bernard-burke&pid=189854971&fhid=10107|title=Bernard Burke Obituary|date=August 9, 2018|website=The Boston Globe|via=Legacy.com|access-date=August 11, 2018}}</ref> He had two sisters, Sarah (Sally) Berenson and Clare Malloy.<ref name="obituary2" />

He went to [[Lexington High School (Massachusetts)|Lexington High School]].<ref name="obituary2" /> Burke studied for an undergraduate physics degree at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT), graduating in 1950, before going on to study for a PhD in physics, graduating again from MIT in 1953.<ref name="nrao_papers" /><ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Finding the Big Bang|last=Burke|first=Bernard F.|date=March 26, 2009|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-51982-3|editor-last=Peebles|editor-first=P. James E.|pages=176–184|language=en|chapter=4.6.1 Bernard F. Burke: Radio astronomy from first contacts to CMBR|editor-last2=Page|editor-first2=Lyman A. Jr.|editor-last3=Partridge|editor-first3=R. Bruce|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QdcdcMi-xpgC&pg=PA176}}</ref>

== Career ==
From 1953 until 1965, he was employed to carry out radio astronomy research by [[Carnegie Institution of Washington]], where he also headed the Radio Astronomy Section from 1962 until 1965. Burke became a faculty member of the Physics department at MIT and later was the [[William A. M. Burden]] Professor of Astrophysics, Emeritus.<ref name="nrao_papers" /><ref name=":0" /> He was a [[principal investigator]] of the [[Kavli Institute]] for Astrophysics and Space Research at MIT.<ref name="obituary">{{cite web|url=https://science.nrao.edu/enews/11.8/index.shtml#burke|title=Bernard (Bernie) F. Burke, 7 June 1928 – 5 August 2018|last=Beasley|first=Tony|date=August 9, 2018|website=NRAO eNews|publisher=Associated Universities, Inc. National Science Foundation|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180810041926/https://science.nrao.edu/enews/11.8/index.shtml|archive-date=August 10, 2018|url-status=live|access-date=August 11, 2018}}</ref>

He served on the National Science Foundation Astronomy Advisory Panel between 1958 and 1963, and the National Radio Astronomy Observatory Visiting Committee in 1958–1962. He was a Trustee for Associated Universities, Inc. between 1972 and 1990. He was also a member of Planetary Systems Working Group and the Towards Other Planetary Systems Scientific Working Group, and he was on advisory councils and committees for the [[National Research Council (United States)|National Research Council]], the [[National Academy of Sciences]], the [[National Science Board]], the [[Keck Telescope]], the [[Naval Studies Board]] and the [[Space Science Board]].<ref name="nrao_papers" />

He was councilor and later president of the [[American Astronomical Society]] in 1971–74 and 1986–88. He was a member of the National Science Foundation Astronomy Advisory Panel in 1958–63.<ref name="obituary" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://aas.org/about/governance/past-officers-and-councilors|title=Past Officers and Trustees|website=American Astronomical Society|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180810105253/https://aas.org/about/governance/past-officers-and-trustees|archive-date=August 10, 2018|access-date=August 11, 2018}}</ref>

== Research ==
[[File:133474main marker lg.jpg|thumb|Roadside historic marker along River Road near the former Seneca Observatory that details a co-discovery of Bernard Flood Burke's.]]
Burke and [[Kenneth Franklin]] discovered [[Decametric radio emissions]] from Jupiter in 1955<ref name="obituary" /> using the [[Mills Cross Array]], while they were trying to observe the [[Crab Nebula]].<ref name="radiojove">{{cite web|url=https://radiojove.gsfc.nasa.gov/library/sci_briefs/discovery.html|title=The Discovery of Jupiter's Radio Emissions|last=Garcia|first=Leonard N.|website=Radio JOVE|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171103150537/https://radiojove.gsfc.nasa.gov/library/sci_briefs/discovery.html|archive-date=November 3, 2017|url-status=live|access-date=August 11, 2018}}</ref> He searched for [[gravitational lenses]],<ref name="nrao_papers" /> and was one of a 6-person team that discovered the first [[Einstein Ring]] in 1988.<ref name="obituary" /><ref name="einsteinring">{{cite journal|title=Unusual radio source MG1131+0456: a possible Einstein ring|author=Hewitt, J. N.|author2=Turner, E. L.|author3=Schneider, D. P.|author4=Burke, B. F.|author5=Langston, G. I.|author6=Lawrence, C. R.|journal=Nature|volume=333|issue=6173|pages=537–540|date=June 9, 1988|doi=10.1038/333537a0|bibcode=1988Natur.333..537H|s2cid=23277001}}</ref>

He also researched exoplanets, and worked on both ground- and space-based [[VLBI]].<ref name="nrao_papers" />

He co-authored ''Introduction to Radio Astronomy'', a textbook that has had three editions, with [[Francis Graham-Smith]].<ref name="nrao_papers" />

Jansky Lecturer at the [[National Radio Astronomy Observatory]] (NRAO), 1998<ref name="nrao_papers" /><ref name="obituary" /> He donated his papers, some linear {{convert|16.5|feet|m}} in size, to the NRAO archives in July–September 2011.<ref name="nrao_papers" />

== Personal life ==
[[File:Bernard Burke.jpg|thumb|Bernie Burke, at the NASA SETI Working Group, UC Berkeley, September 1981]]
He spent time hiking in the [[White Mountains (New Hampshire)|White Mountains]] and the [[Rocky Mountains]], and sailing from [[Marblehead, Massachusetts|Marblehead]]. He also enjoyed [[chess]].<ref name="obituary2" />

He was married to Jane Pann Burke, and later to Elizabeth (Betsy) Platt. He had a daughter, Elizabeth Kahn, and three sons, Mark, Geoffrey, and Matthew. He had 8 grand children and 1 great-grandchild at the time of his death.<ref name="obituary2" /> He died on August 5, 2018.<ref name="obituary" />

== Recognition ==
In 1963, Burke received The [[Helen B. Warner Prize for Astronomy]]. He was also a member of several academic and honorary societies including [[American Astronomical Society]], [[American Physical Society]], [[International Astronomical Union]], [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], American Academy for the Advancement of Science, International Scientific Radio Union U.S. National Committee – Commission J.<ref name="nrao_papers" /> In 1970, Burke was elected to [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="nrao_papers" /><ref name="obituary" />
